text: Design a frequency stack. Push adds a value; pop removes and returns the most frequent value. If several tie, return the one closest to the top — the most recently pushed.
Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — two rules in order: highest frequency first, then among ties, most recent. Right?

The neat idea is to layer by frequency. Keep a stack for each frequency level. When a value is pushed, its frequency rises, and I drop it into that level's stack. The top of the highest non-empty level is both the most frequent and, among ties, the most recent.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive pop scans everything for the max frequency and then needs insertion times for ties — linear per pop, and awkward. This problem reminds me of bucketing by count, like a bucket sort over frequencies — except each bucket is a stack, so recency comes for free. Frequency-layered stacks give both rules at once, in amortized constant time if I track the max frequency as an integer.

Here's the plan. One: keep a count per value, and a stack per frequency level. Two: push bumps the count to f and pushes the value onto level f. Three: pop takes the top of the highest level and decrements that value's count. One thing worth flagging — a value with frequency three sits in levels one, two, and three simultaneously. So after I pop it off the top level and decrement its frequency, its copies in lower levels keep it in play. And the level being a stack is exactly what breaks ties by recency — no timestamps needed. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. A hash map holds each value's count, and an ordered map goes from frequency to a stack of values. Push increments the count and pushes onto that level. Pop reads the largest key with r-begin, takes that stack's top, and decrements the count. One thing worth flagging — I erase a level once it's empty, so r-begin keeps pointing at a real highest level. Replacing the ordered map with a hash map plus an integer max frequency, decremented when the top level empties, makes it constant time.

Let's dry-run: push five, seven, five, seven, four, five, then four pops. After the pushes, level one holds five, seven, four; level two holds five, seven; level three holds five. The rows that matter are pops two and three, both at level two: that stack is five then seven, so it returns seven, the more recent, then five. Only when level two empties does it drop to level one and return four. The sequence five, seven, five, four matches, with recency handled purely by stack order. Corner cases: all-distinct pushes all have frequency one, so pop behaves like a plain stack. A single value pushed three times comes back three times, dropping one level per pop.

The time complexity is log D per operation with the ordered map, where D is the number of distinct frequency levels, or amortized constant with the max-frequency integer variant. The space complexity is linear — each push stores one copy in one level. Oh, one more thing — if ties should instead take the oldest, I'd make each level a queue instead of a stack; the rest is identical.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You layered by frequency, so a value lives in several levels at once. You saw the top of the highest level satisfies both rules with no timestamps. And you gave the constant-time max-frequency refinement and the queue swap for the opposite tie-break. Good work.
